slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the lesson's growth-rate table yourself: compute O(n), O(n^2), and O(2^n) at n=100 by hand or calculator, confirming O(2^n) comes out to roughly 1.27 x 10^30. slots.practicalActivity: Write out the containment chain P subset-of BPP subset-of BQP subset-of PSPACE, with one sentence justifying each inclusion in your own words. slots.practicalActivity: Compute Grover's query count for N=1,000,000 using floor((pi/4)*sqrt(N)) by hand, confirming the lesson's figure of 785 queries versus classical's up to 1,000,000. slots.practicalActivity: Apply the lesson's four-question classification checklist yourself to the Check Yourself's graph-coloring problem ('can this graph's nodes be colored with k colors so no two adjacent nodes share a color?'), walking through each of the four questions explicitly and reaching a final classification with a stated quantum-advantage verdict. slots.practicalActivity: Hand-compute the full 4x4 DFT matrix entry by entry using F_kj = (1/sqrt(4)) * e^(2*pi*i*j*k/4), confirming it matches the lesson's verified matrix exactly (row 0 all 0.5, row 2 alternating signs). lessons.title: Why QFT Is Exponentially Faster — and What That Doesn't Mean

slots.practicalActivity: Write a worked rebuttal to the lesson's Check Yourself classmate who claims O(n^2) gates vs O(n*2^n) operations means you should 'always use a quantum computer' to Fourier-transform data -- name specifically the readout problem and why a single measurement destroying N-1 amplitudes defeats that claim. Then list, in your own words, the two example algorithms (phase estimation, Shor's) that structurally avoid this readout problem and explain how each one does.
slots.deliverable: A written rebuttal to the classmate's overclaim naming the readout problem specifically, plus a two-item list explaining how phase estimation and Shor's algorithm each sidestep it.

slots.practicalActivity: Hand-trace the n=2 QFT circuit (H(q1), Controlled-R2, H(q2), SWAP) applied to |3> = |q1=1,q2=1>, following the exact four-step method the lesson used for |1> and |2>, and state your final amplitude vector in the a|0>+b|1>+c|2>+d|3> form. slots.practicalActivity: Write a concrete answer to the lesson's Check Yourself: explain specifically why diagonalizing U as an explicit matrix stops being realistic once U acts on 50 qubits (compute how large a 2^50 x 2^50 matrix actually is), and explain in your own words why phase estimation's 'apply-only, never-inspect' black-box access pattern is exactly the regime that situation requires.
slots.deliverable: A written answer computing the scale of a 2^50-dimensional matrix and explaining why black-box phase estimation, not classical diagonalization, is the only realistic approach at that scale.

slots.practicalActivity: Work through the lesson's Check Yourself phase-kickback algebra by hand for phi=pi (U|psi> = -|psi>): starting from control qubit (|0>+|1>)/sqrt(2) and target |psi>, apply controlled-U and show the resulting state, confirming the target register is still exactly |psi> while the control qubit's phase has flipped to (|0>-|1>)/sqrt(2).

slots.practicalActivity: Using the theta=0.3, n=3 probability table from the lesson, verify the eight probabilities sum to exactly 1 (add them up yourself). lessons.title: Phase Estimation as a Building Block for Other Algorithms

lessons.title: Optimal Iteration Count — and Why More Isn't Better

lessons.title: Why Breaking RSA Today Is Not Practical

lessons.title: Capstone: the Quantum Algorithms Laboratory Project

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can place any computational problem into P, NP-complete, BQP-with-known-speedup, or no-known-quantum-advantage using a repeatable checklist, has derived and hand-verified the QFT, phase estimation, Grover's algorithm, and Shor's algorithm with real numeric examples rather than taken-on-faith formulas, and can honestly benchmark a quantum algorithm against its best classical competitor instead of overselling a speedup claim.
